sources.summary: Balanced interferometer: unobstructed arms permit a dark output; opaque obstruction changes outcomes. A successful dark-output single-photon detection excludes that photon being absorbed or scattered by the object. Other outcomes include absorption and inconclusive detection. Interpretation of zero interaction is qualified explicitly.
limits: Theory and ideal apparatus; real alignment, leakage and detector noise matter.
No preferred path or interpretation asserted. No general zero disturbance claim.

sources.summary: Authors explain two-path interference, a dark output, and object-induced changes. They describe a heralded single-photon experiment with a Michelson implementation and a deflecting mirror as the obstacle. Dark-output clicks demonstrate the effect, with finite leakage and unsuccessful outcomes.
limits: Participant explanation, not independent replication or raw data review.
Production uses an ideal Mach-Zehnder absorbing-obstacle model, not a replica of their Michelson mirror experiment.
1995 PRL researcher PDF was image-only: fetched and attempted text extraction, but body not inspected; not used as verified evidence.

definitions: In an ideal aligned single-photon interferometer, a successful dark-output click can reveal an opaque obstacle without that photon being absorbed or scattered by it.
Operational successful-trial statement; no metaphysical zero interaction or guarantee.
A balanced interferometer offers two possible paths that recombine.
Path wave amplitudes, not two half photons or classical definite trajectories.
With both arms unobstructed and correct alignment, destructive interference makes one output dark in the ideal model.
Real leakage and detector noise prevent absolute experimental certainty.
The amplitudes associated with the two arms cancel at that output.
Schematic waves represent probability amplitudes, not visible light or destroyed photon energy.
An object that absorbs the single photon prevents it reaching either output detector.
One photon, ideal absorber and output detectors; not all detectors in actual heralding apparatus.
Blocking one arm makes a formerly dark output possible in the ideal model.
Sometimes, not every trial; no unqualified practical detector certainty.
Other trials result in photon absorption or inconclusive bright-output detection.
This simple arrangement risks absorption; no universally harmless sensing claim.
Researchers have experimentally demonstrated interaction-free measurement.
Participant account describes different physical implementation; original research figures and raw data not inspected.
Interaction-free measurement proves that nothing interacts anywhere in every interpretation.
Unverified overreach explicitly excluded; source discusses interpretation dependence.
lines: How can light reveal an obstacle without being absorbed or reflected by it?
Send one photon into an interferometer: two possible paths, joined again.
With both paths open and the device correctly aligned, interference keeps one detector dark.
The waves associated with the two paths cancel at that output.
Now put a light-absorbing object in one path. If it absorbs the photon, neither output detector clicks.
But sometimes the formerly dark detector clicks instead.
That single photon reached the detector, so the object did not absorb it. The blocked path removed the cancellation.
The click reveals the obstacle. Other trials absorb the photon or give no clear answer. This is not a guaranteed harmless test.
Researchers have demonstrated this effect, called interaction-free measurement. The clue comes from changing which paths are available.
objectives: Present the operational puzzle: obstacle absorption excluded in the detected outcome.
Establish one photon and two coherent alternatives, not split photon energy.
Set up dark detector baseline in ideal aligned model.
Show opposed amplitude contributions at the output.
Show absorber and separately labeled absorbed trial.
Return to a successful dark-output trial, conditional not universal.
Connect detected photon to absence of absorption, and blocked-path loss of cancellation.
Show all three ideal-model outcomes; retain risk and inconclusive trial.
Return to the successful outcome and name experimentally demonstrated effect.
